allprojects.name: Found Footage Creep
allprojects.description: FFC is a database app of information related to found footage movies. Here you'll be able to find a big set of movies of found footage genre. In total there are more than 1,000 movies, shorts and videos. You can create your own watchlist in order to never forget your favourite found footage movies and you can keep track of the ones you like.
allprojects.roadmap:
As a huge fan of the found footage genre, I've always found it surprisingly difficult to track information about these films. While there are plenty of general movie databases, none of them specifically cater to the unique characteristics of this niche. This frustration was the initial spark for building this Android app. I wanted a centralized hub where I could not only find details like plots, actors, and ratings but also manage my personal watchlist and 'likes' for a genre I'm passionate about. 

 Developing this app, however, presented some interesting challenges. The first major hurdle was scraping movie information from IMDb and formatting it into a clean CSV file to populate my initial database. This required careful parsing and data cleaning to ensure accuracy. Once the data was prepped, the next challenge was writing and executing the numerous SQLite commands to handle core functionality: saving and retrieving movies, adding and removing them from a personal watchlist, and managing favorites. I also had to implement SharedPreferences to persist the state of the 'like' buttons since it's a simpler and more efficient way to store small amounts of data, while SQLite is useful for storing large amounts of structured data. I also had to manage passing data between different activities within the app. For example, I had to ensure that when a user tapped on a movie from the main list, the correct information was sent to the details screen. Navigating these complexities pushed me to deepen my understanding of database operations, data persistence, data filtering, and inter-component communication in Android. 

 The primary lesson I took away from this project was the importance of user-centric design, even for a personal project. By building an app to solve my own problem, I was forced to consider the user's journey from their perspective. I learned that meticulous planning and a well-structured database are the bedrock of any robust application. This experience has significantly influenced my approach to subsequent projects. If I were to do it all over again, I would likely explore using a more modern persistence library like Room, which would have streamlined the database interactions and reduced a significant amount of boilerplate code.
functionalities: Movie filtering by movie title or director
Movie sorting by release date, movie rating and by name
Insert and remove movies from watchlist
Insert and remove movies from favourites
Consult movie information

allprojects.name: CoolReads
allprojects.description: CoolReads is a web application inspired by Goodreads, and it was designed for managing personal libraries, track the reading progress, consult book informations and connect with other reader lovers. The aim was to build a platform more user-friendly, easier to manage collections and more social engaging.
allprojects.roadmap:
The genesis of CoolReads was born from a common users' frustration with existing book-tracking platforms. While Goodreads is a powerful tool, users find the interface outdated and its social features clunky. The porpuse was to build a modern, intuitive, and highly social platform that would not only help me manage personal library collections but also connect with a vibrant community of fellow book lovers. The goal was to create a space where the joy of reading could be shared and celebrated in a more engaging way.

The development of CoolReads presented a number of significant challenges, particularly in the realm of full-stack integration and performance. A key hurdle was orchestrating the complex backend architecture using Java and Spring Boot to communicate seamlessly with a dynamic Vue.js frontend. In that way, a robust REST API was designed to handle a multiple user actions, from adding books to a shelf, tracking reading progress, submitting reviews and reactions. The project required a deep understanding of Spring Security for secure authentication, Spring Data JPA for efficient database interactions with PostgreSQL, and Redis for in-memory caching to boost performance. The sheer number of moving parts—frontend, backend, database, and cache—demanded meticulous planning and debugging to ensure every feature worked in harmony.

This project had a complete full-stack development and DevOps development. It taught critical importance of a well-defined layered architecture for building scalable and maintainable applications. It was a good project to handle containerized services with Docker and orchestrate them with Kubernetes, creating a robust and scalable deployment pipeline on Google Cloud. The load testing with JMeter was particularly insightful, as it exposed performance bottlenecks and validated the use of Redis for caching. Looking back, I would definitely integrate a third-party books API service to populate the platform with real data and also to stress the pod instances of our backend and see how our application would perform. Furthermore, it would be interesting to explore a more microservices-oriented architecture to break up our monolithic backend service, which could improve scalability and resilience. Other final remaining challenge would be to complete the social functionalities as planned in the initial user requirements.
functionalities: Book search
Search books by category
Interact and review books
Rate books
Consult book statistics (the percentage of default bookshelves the book is present, the gender percentage who read the book, etc.)
Consult book information (rating,writer,publisher,plot,etc.)
Handle books from personal bookshelves
Profile editing

allprojects.name: Virtual Map of Braga
allprojects.description: A web application featuring a virtual map of Braga's streets and their historical context. This application features a set of features that allow you to add and remove locations, cross-navigation through streets, and search for street's information.
allprojects.roadmap:
I developed a Braga Street Map as a robust full-stack application to create a searchable, interactive database of streets in Braga, Portugal. The goal was to transform a static, disorganized collection of data and pictures taken by biomedical students into a dynamic platform that would allow users to explore information about streets, view related locations, and engage with the system by adding their own comments and content. This project was a practical application of building a complete, end-to-end solution, from raw data to a user-friendly interface.

The biggest challenge in this project was managing a highly interconnected dataset and building a scalable architecture around it. The data was separated through 60 XML files, each containing detailed information about a single street and streets related. The first major hurdle was parsing all this data and converting it into a clean JSON format suitable for import into a MongoDB database. The next challenge was maintaining consistency and integrity for street relationships—specifically, ensuring that when one street was added or removed, all references to it in other 'related streets' were accurately updated. I had to design a robust API using Express.js to handle these complex data manipulations.

This project was a deep dive into containerization by modularize the application by separating it into four distinct services: an authentication service, a streets API service, a frontend, and the database. By Dockerizing each service and linking them on a network bridge, I was able to manage their communication and dependencies effectively. This approach not only made the application more resilient and scalable but also streamlined my development and deployment workflow. It taught me the invaluable lesson of breaking down complex systems into manageable, independent components. If I were to improve this project, I would integrate a real-time map service in order to give the user a more immersive experience and see how the street evoluted and not rely only on the picture took.
functionalities: Consult street information
Handle street information
Comment streets

allprojects.name: Bargain Hunter
allprojects.description: Bargain-hunter is an android app that scans the latest and nearest sales of products in Braga.
allprojects.roadmap:
I developed Bargain-Hunter as a solution for a common local problem: how to easily find the latest and best product sales in my city, Braga. Existing solutions were either too broad or required manual effort. I wanted to create a simple yet powerful tool that would automatically find these deals and, most importantly, notify me when a great sale was happening nearby. This project combined my interests in mobile development, data engineering, and leveraging cloud services to create a truly practical, hyper-local application.

The primary technical challenge was building the automated system for data collection. I couldn't rely on existing APIs, so I had to implement a data-scraping pipeline from scratch. This involved writing a Python script to scrape a set of product sales from a specific website daily. I then had to figure out how to automate this process reliably. My solution was to deploy the script on a Google Cloud VM, scheduling it to execute daily. The data was then seamlessly pushed to a Firebase Database, which served as the backend for the Android app. This required me to integrate the app with Firebase and configure notifications to alert users about new sales. The most significant challenge was working with synthetic location data, as the website didn't provide real addresses. This forced me to come up with a workaround to make the 'nearest' sales feature functional, even if not perfectly precise.

This project was a fantastic exercise in full-stack development, with a strong focus on backend automation and cloud integration. I learned how to build a robust, serverless-like architecture using Google Cloud and Firebase, demonstrating proficiency in both cloud infrastructure and mobile development. The experience taught me the importance of data quality; even though i extracted real data for product info like name, price and images; the location was generated and consists of synthetic data. This highlighted the limitations of working with imperfect information. If I were to improve this project, I would focus on adapting the scraping script to extract real, precise location data from the websites, which would significantly enhance the app's core value proposition by providing genuinely accurate 'nearest' sales notifications. This would be a crucial next step in transforming the app from a proof of concept into a fully polished, production-ready product.
functionalities: Check list of sales
Check list of top nearby sales
Search filters of product sales
Consult product's information
Consult statistics of sales in Braga

allprojects.name: filmz
allprojects.description: filmz is a web application for consulting film information and managing personal collections of watchlists and liked movies.
allprojects.roadmap:
I built Filmz as a personal project to create a comprehensive, single-source web application for film enthusiasts. My goal was to move beyond generic movie sites and develop a platform that was not only a rich source of information but also a powerful tool for personal movie management. By integrating with the TMDB API, I aimed to provide a dynamic and constantly updated experience, allowing users to explore trending films, build watchlists, and manage their 'liked' movies all in one place.

The most significant challenge was orchestrating the front-end and back-end to work in a cohesive, responsive manner. I used the Express framework to build a robust API that could fetch, process, and serve data from the TMDB API. On the front end, I used Pug to render dynamic HTML and AJAX calls to implement a smooth, modern user experience. The key technical hurdle was implementing pagination with AJAX—updating the movie grid without a full page reload, which required careful handling of data requests and DOM manipulation. I also tackled the complexities of displaying a movie's trailer within a jQuery modal, ensuring a seamless pop-up video experience. Authentication was another challenge, as I had to learn how to generate and use tokens via the TMDB API to securely manage user sessions for personal collections.

This project was an excellent learning experience in full-stack web development. It provided hands-on practice with API integration, back-end development with Node.js and Express, and creating a dynamic, interactive front-end with Pug and AJAX. I learned the importance of optimizing data flow to improve user experience. The use of jQuery modals and AJAX taught me how to create a more efficient and polished interface. This experience solidified my understanding of how a front-end and back-end communicate to deliver a seamless user experience. If I were to tackle this project again, I would explore migrating the front end to a modern framework like Vue.js or React to handle state management more efficiently and potentially implement server-side rendering for better performance and SEO.
functionalities: Authentication through token and session generation according to TMDB api
Movie pagination of what's trending
Movie search by title
Pagination of actors
Handle watchlists and favourites
Whatch movie trailers
Consult movie informations and gallery

allprojects.name: ASCN-LARAVELIO
allprojects.description: Automation of the deployment, configuration and monitoring of the Laravel.io application.
allprojects.roadmap:
This project was a deep dive into the practical application of modern DevOps principles. The goal was to take a pre-existing application, Laravel.io, and create a robust, scalable, and fully automated deployment pipeline on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). It was a three-phase journey: first, containerizing the application; second, automating its deployment and configuration; and finally, setting up a system for monitoring and auto-scaling. This project wasn't about building an application from scratch, but about mastering the tools and processes that make modern software delivery efficient and reliable.

The core challenge was orchestrating the complex interactions between different cloud and containerization technologies. The first hurdle was to Dockerize the Laravel application, which involved creating a container that could be deployed consistently across environments. Next, was necessary automating the setup on GKE. This required writing Ansible playbooks to manage tasks such as creating and deleting Kubernetes pods, configuring the MySQL database, and injecting environment variables. This automation was critical for ensuring that the deployment was repeatable and consistent. Finally, the most advanced challenge was implementing auto-scaling. In that order, horizontal scaling was done using HorizontalPodAutoscaler to provision new replicas of the application when a certain CPU consumption threshold was reached, ensuring the application could handle increased user load without manual intervention.

This project was an invaluable learning experience in DevOps, containerization, and cloud-native architecture. It provided hands-on expertise with key industry tools like Docker, Kubernetes, and Ansible. The use of JMeter for load testing taught me how to simulate real-world traffic to identify performance bottlenecks and validate the effectiveness of the auto-scaling strategy. This project solidified my understanding of how to build and maintain resilient, high-the project again, I would also integrate a tool like Vault to securely manage and distribute sensitive information, such as API keys and database credentials, to the application's various components.
functionalities: Packaging the Laravel.io application into a Docker containers for consistent deployment.
Using Ansible to automate tasks like creating and removing application pods and configuring the MySQL database
Deploying and managing the application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to handle container orchestration
Using Google Cloud Monitoring API to observe the application's performance metrics
Automatically provisioning new application replicas based on CPU consumption to handle increased load
Using JMeter to simulate user traffic and stress-test the application

allprojects.name: Ctack-0M
allprojects.description: A stack-based programming language interpreter built from scratch in C. The project processes and executes commands for mathematical expressions, variable assignments, and complex data manipulations, demonstrating a deep understanding of data structures and low-level programming principles.
allprojects.roadmap:
This project was a deep dive into the fundamentals of computer science by implementing a stack-based programming language interpreter from scratch. The goal was to build a system that could read commands from standard input, execute them based on a stack-oriented architecture, and print the final state of the stack. This was a challenge to not only understand how interpreters work under the hood but also to master low-level memory management and data structures using the C programming language.

The most significant challenge was the sheer complexity of managing all the different operations and data types on a single stack. A robust system design was implemented to handle everything from basic arithmetic and bitwise operations to complex logic, array manipulations, and variable assignment. A major technical hurdle was maintaining a clean and correct data state. For instance, implementing the _ (duplicate) and \ (swap) operations required careful manipulation of stack pointers to avoid memory leaks or data corruption. The project was broken down into several phases, each with its own set of challenges, from implementing basic mathematical expressions and stack manipulation to handling complex logical conditions and I/O.

This project had practical application of abstract data structures. I gained a deep understanding of how a stack works and how to use it to evaluate complex expressions. The process of building this project from the ground up, with dedicated components for stack operations, parsing, and type conversions, taught me the importance of modular and well-structured code. It solidified my knowledge of memory management and low-level programming, which is a rare and valuable skill. If I were to do this again, I would explore adding more advanced features like function definitions and calls, which would require implementing a call stack in addition to the data stack, pushing the project to an even more advanced level.

allprojects.name: ProjetoLI3-2021-22
allprojects.description: This project is a high-performance software solution written in C that efficiently processes and queries large-volume CSV files. It features a custom-built data management system and uses advanced data structures like hash tables to handle complex queries and optimize memory usage, exploring low-level programming, data manipulation in C, and performance measuring.
allprojects.roadmap:
This project was a deep dive into high-performance data management and memory optimization in C. The objective was to build a software solution capable of executing a series of complex queries on large-volume CSV files. In this project, SGR (Repository Management System), we customed a C struct designed to efficiently store and access user, commit, and repository data. This project was a practical exercise in building a data processing pipeline from the ground up, focusing on speed and resource management.

The primary challenge was managing large datasets and optimizing memory usage, a crucial task given the size of the CSV files. We had to architect a system that could read and process vast amounts of data without crashing. A significant hurdle was the implementation of Query 5, which required building a hash table as the commits file was parsed. This hash table, a core component of the catalogos_commit struct, was used to map commit authors to their respective commit counts. Another major challenge was the validation logic, which caused the program to crash when validating multiple files simultaneously. This forced me to meticulously debug and refine my data handling and validation functions.

Through this project, I gained invaluable experience in low-level programming and data structures. I learned to use the GLib library to implement robust data structures like hash tables, which was crucial for efficient data storage and retrieval. My memory management skills were significantly enhanced as I had to debug crashes and optimize the code to handle large files. This project also introduced me to concepts like encapsulation and Model-View-Controller (MVC) architectural pattern in a C context, which helped me structure the codebase logically. We also used libraries like time.h for performance profiling, allowing to measure and improve the execution time of each query.

allprojects.name: Monitoring and Recording System for Information on Home Energy Consumption - SmartHouses
allprojects.description: SmartHouses is a system for monitoring and recording information about the energy consumption of multiple houses. In each of these houses, the user can observe the various compartments and smart equipment belonging to the owner, and also perform certain manipulations and simulations in the daily consumption system for different suppliers.
allprojects.roadmap:
I developed SmartHouses as a robust system for monitoring and managing the energy consumption of multiple homes. The goal was to provide a comprehensive platform where users could view their homes' various compartments and smart equipment, track energy usage, and even perform simulations. This project was a practical and intensive exercise in applying core object-oriented programming (OOP) principles to build a maintainable and scalable application.

The primary architectural challenge was to faithfully implement the MVC Delegate (Model-View-Controller) pattern. This required a clear separation of concerns, ensuring the Model held all the business logic and data, the View handled all user interactions, and the Controller acted as the intermediary. This design choice forced me to think modularly, making the codebase easier to manage. Beyond the architecture, a key challenge was consistently applying OOP principles to ensure code quality. For example, I used encapsulation to control data access, which proved crucial as the project evolved. This made the code more resilient to changes and far more reusable. Similarly, inheritance allowed me to avoid code duplication by having specialized objects inherit from a base class, while polymorphism was essential for handling different types of smart devices with a unified set of methods.

This project was a foundational learning experience in software design. It solidified my understanding of how a well-structured codebase, built on principles like encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism, leads to a more robust and elegant program. I learned that these concepts aren't just theoretical; they are practical tools for solving real-world development problems. The experience of building and maintaining a complex system from a well-defined architectural pattern taught me to write code that is not only functional but also easy to debug, modify, and extend. A key area for improvement would be to integrate the system with real-time data streams from actual IoT devices, rather than relying on simulated data. This would transform the project into a live monitoring tool and provide a new set of challenges related to data processing, latency, and real-time updates.
functionalities: Show the house that used the most energy in a period of time
Highest-billing supplier
List of invoices issued by supplier
Order of the biggest energy consumers during a period of time
Manage devices in a house (add and remove smartbulbs, smartspeaker, smartcamera, change lamp hue, change speaker volume, turn devices on and off)
Simulation of the passage of a period of time with device operations in several houses and respective calculation of operating statistics.

allprojects.name: JMaster
allprojects.description: JMaster is an application for learning and deepening your knowledge in Japanese. This is an application for all those who want to master and study the Japanese language. In this app you can find hiragana and katakana quizzes, dictionary, as well as N4 and N5 kanji. There is a complementary section with listening and reading exercises.
allprojects.roadmap:
I developed JMaster as a personal project to create a comprehensive mobile application for anyone looking to learn or master the Japanese language. The goal was to build a single, easy-to-use platform that would provide a range of learning tools, including hiragana and katakana quizzes, a dictionary, and a collection of N4 and N5 Kanji. I wanted to create a convenient, on-the-go study aid that I and others could use to deepen our understanding of the language.

The main technical challenge was designing and implementing a robust data structure to support the application's features, particularly the dictionary and quizzes. I chose to use a Firebase Realtime Database to store the vast amount of dictionary entries. This required me to structure the data efficiently to enable queries for features like the dictionary search. Another hurdle was designing the user interface to be intuitive and clean, ensuring that the app felt accessible to beginners while still providing enough depth for more advanced learners. I also added a drawing kanji feature, even though it still needs to recognize kanji input strokes.

This project was a fantastic exercise in Android development and mobile backend integration. I gained hands-on experience in building a complete application from start to finish, from UI/UX design to backend data management with Firebase. It solidified my understanding of how to build interactive educational tools and manage large datasets efficiently in a mobile environment. A key lesson I learned was the importance of user-centric design—making sure the flow of a language learning app feels natural and rewarding. Looking back, a valuable next step would be to implement a feature for users to save custom word lists to their personal accounts, as this would provide a more personalized and flexible learning experience. If I were to improve this project, I would focus on adding more robust speech recognition and natural language processing (NLP) features for more interactive listening and reading exercises.
functionalities: Japanese word search with direct application in sentences and pronunciation (dictionary)
Hiragana and katakana quiz
Kanji pronunciation and meaning
Kanji drawing
Note taking
Multiple choice listening exercises
Story section with pronunciation

allprojects.name: SD22-23
allprojects.description: A client-server service for managing scooter fleets in Braga. This service will allow multiple users to reserve scooters and park them after a certain amount of time has passed after reaching their final destination. To ensure that scooters are spaced out and accessible to all, the system will award rewards to users who travel to specific locations. Additionally, this system will allow each user to receive notifications of potential rewards originating within a fixed distance of a given location.
allprojects.roadmap:
I developed a multithreaded server-client system to explore concurrent programming and network communication protocols. The core challenge of this project was to build a robust and scalable server that could handle multiple client connections simultaneously while adhering to a specific requirement: no server thread should write to more than one socket. This led me to implement a Thread Per Connection paradigm, where each new client connection triggers the creation of a dedicated thread to manage its requests. The server listens on a single socket to accept all incoming connections.

The technical implementation of this system involved designing a custom communication protocol in a binary format, using DataInputStream and DataOutputStream to send and receive byte streams over the network. A crucial part of this protocol was the TaggedConnection class. Each request and response was assigned a unique tag, allowing the server to correctly correlate them. To ensure the server knew how much data to read, the size of each data frame was written to the socket before the data itself. On the client side, a Demultiplexer class was created to manage the asynchronous nature of the communication, using a Map to store and identify requests by their tags, and blocking a thread until a corresponding response was received. This approach was essential for preventing deadlocks and ensuring a smooth user experience as they navigated the application's menu-based interface. To prevent users from reserving the same scooter simultaneously, I implemented some critical sections using a lock to block and guarantee mutual exclusion. This ensured that from the moment a free scooter was identified to the point it was marked as occupied, no other thread could interfere, thereby preventing race conditions.

This project was an intensive learning experience in network programming, concurrency, and low-level data serialization. It taught me the complexities of managing shared resources in a multithreaded environment and the importance of a well-defined communication protocol. I gained a deep understanding of how threads, sockets, and data streams work together to build a responsive client-server application. The use of a Demultiplexer and a Thread Per Connection model was particularly insightful, as it provided a concrete example of a design pattern for handling concurrent requests.
functionalities: List of available scooters located on a map
Scooter reservation for a period of time
To ensure a good distribution of scooters across the map, a reward generation mechanism was created

When notifications are activated, the customer is asked the radius of the location in which they would like to be notified of the existence of new rewards, as well as the time interval in which they wish to receive these notifications
User authentication mechanism

allprojects.name: DAA-2324
allprojects.description: Exploration, modeling and analysis of a dataset predicting energy injection into the grid according to meteorological factors, and of a diamond classification dataset using machine learning strategies and algorithms.
allprojects.roadmap:
This project was a deep dive into the world of machine learning, focusing on the exploration, modeling, and analysis of two distinct datasets. The objective was to apply a variety of supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms to solve both regression and classification problems, and then to critically evaluate their performance. This hands-on experience was a practical application of theoretical concepts, allowing me to understand the strengths and weaknesses of different models in a real-world context.

The main challenge was not just in applying the models, but in the entire machine learning pipeline: from data preprocessing and feature engineering to model training and performance evaluation. We had to select appropriate metrics for each problem type—such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and R-squared (R2) for regression, and accuracy for classification—and interpret the results to compare model effectiveness. For instance, in the diamond dataset, while a simple Decision Tree Regressor performed well, the Stacking Ensemble Learning model achieved the highest R2 value, demonstrating the power of combining multiple models. Similarly, for classification, we compared the performance of models like Decision Tree, SVM, and Neural Networks, gaining insight into their respective strengths. Another challenge was fine-tuning model hyperparameters to prevent overfitting and improve generalization.

This project solidified my understanding of the machine learning workflow. It taught me the importance of not relying on a single algorithm but instead experimenting with a variety of models to find the best fit for a given dataset. I learned how to use powerful techniques like ensemble learning (Random Forest, Boosting) to achieve superior performance compared to individual models. The experience with different metrics provided a nuanced understanding of model evaluation beyond simple accuracy. Furthermore work should be done at preprocessing level in order to see if the models can predict with higher accuracy.

allprojects.name: Racing Manager
allprojects.description: Racing Manager is a system in Java that allows you to simulate car racing championships. The genesis of the application is similar to the F1 Manager game.
allprojects.roadmap:
Racing Manager is a comprehensive car racing simulation system inspired by games like F1 Manager. At its core, it’s a multiplayer game where registered users compete in simulated championships. The goal was to build a robust, multi-tiered application that would manage everything from user roles and championship creation to realistic race simulations and scorekeeping. This project was a deep dive into object-oriented design and creating a layered, maintainable software architecture.

The main challenge was designing and implementing a clean, scalable architecture to manage the complexity of the game's data and logic. We structured the application into three distinct layers using the DAO (Data Access Object) pattern: RacingManagerDL for data persistence, RacingManagerLN for business logic, and RacingManagerUI for the user interface. This separation was critical for ensuring that changes in one layer wouldn't affect the others. The use of the DAO pattern with MariaDB was particularly challenging, as we had to create a robust system for storing and retrieving complex objects like cars, drivers, and championship data while ensuring data integrity and efficiency. Implementing the game's core mechanics, such as race simulation with dynamic events like overtaking and accidents, also presented a significant logical challenge, requiring careful calculation and state management.

This project was an excellent learning experience in software architecture, object-oriented design, and database management. It taught me the importance of a well-defined layered architecture for building complex applications. By using the DAO pattern, I gained practical experience in abstracting data persistence, which is a valuable skill for building scalable and testable applications. The project also honed my skills in Java and MariaDB, particularly in managing data transactions and complex queries. If I were to improve this project, I would integrate an advanced graphical user interface instead of the current text-based console. For example, I could use JavaFX or Swing to create a rich UI with dashboards for race data, car configuration screens, and interactive championship standings. This would significantly improve the user experience and make the simulation feel more like a modern game. Additionally, I would implement a more robust and realistic physics engine for the race simulation.
functionalities: Creating drivers, cars, championships and race tracks
Racing simulation
Consulting global and individual rankings
Account registration
Changing game versions

allprojects.name: JSONfy
allprojects.description: JSONfy is a tool that reads TOML input data and converts it to JSON format. This tool was built with lex and yacc submodules from ply. In each GIC semantic action, data structures such as dictionaries and lists were manipulated in order to produce the resulting JSON.
allprojects.roadmap:
I developed JSONfy, a command-line tool designed to convert data from TOML (Tom's Obvious, Minimal Language) format to JSON. The project's core purpose was to build a robust and reliable parser that could handle the nuances of the TOML specification and output well-formed JSON. This was a fantastic opportunity to delve into the principles of compiler design and language parsing.

The main technical challenge was in implementing the parser from scratch. I used PLY (Python Lex-Yacc), which allowed me to separate the process into two key components: the lexer and the parser. The lexer (using lex) was responsible for tokenizing the input TOML file, identifying key-value pairs, strings, numbers, and other language constructs. The parser (using yacc) then took these tokens and, through a series of semantic actions, built the final JSON data structure. Inside these semantic actions, I had to carefully manage Python dictionaries and lists to accurately represent TOML's nested tables, arrays of tables, and various data types. This required a deep understanding of both TOML's syntax and how to map it to JSON's structure.

This project was an excellent learning experience in language parsing and compiler design fundamentals. It taught me how to break down a complex task like data conversion into manageable, logical steps using tools like PLY. The project also honed my skills in data structure manipulation and algorithmic thinking. The two usage options—one to generate a JSON file and another to serve the data via a simulated RESTful API with Json Server—demonstrate a practical application of the tool beyond simple conversion. If I were to improve this project, I would add more extensive error handling to provide clearer, more specific feedback to the user when an invalid TOML file is provided, and I would also consider supporting additional input formats for greater versatility.
functionalities: Convert json data to toml data
Serve the json data converted with json-server to a REST API

allprojects.name: ProbUM
allprojects.description: ProbUM is a web app that allows teachers to create assessment tests and schedule them, allows students to take them (in a properly scheduled manner), and allows these tests to be graded, typically automatically depending on the type of question.
allprojects.roadmap:
RAS-PROBUM is a full-stack web application for creating and administering online exams. The goal was to build a robust and scalable platform that could manage the entire exam lifecycle, from user authentication, exam creation and realization to real-time result delivery. This project was a comprehensive exercise in modern software architecture, focusing on a microservices-based approach to ensure the system could handle a high volume of concurrent users and complex data interactions.

The main technical challenge was designing a truly decoupled, microservices architecture, instead of a monolithic application. It was built four distinct microservices—exams,users,notifications and rooms—each with a single, dedicated responsibility. A central API Gateway served as the single entry point for all client requests, routing them to the appropriate service, and the point of intercommunication between microservices dependencies. This design was crucial for scalability and maintainability. To handle the real-time nature of notification, it was implemented WebSockets for instant communication between the client and server. The use of a MongoDB database provided a flexible data model for storing exam questions and user data, while SMTP was integrated for sending crucial email notifications, such as exam invitations and results.

 this project I gained invaluable experience in microservices architecture, learning how to design and manage services and the communication between them. allprojects.name: CP-TPG
allprojects.description: In this project were used profiling tools to analyze code performance like gprof and perf. Based on the results obtained, were performed several optimizations at the code logic level, compiler level, and memory hierarchy level (cache). To explore greater parallelism, was used OpenMP to optimize execution time by launching multiple threads (fine-grained parallelism) and to study the scalability of our solution, taking into account load balancing, among other metrics. In the final stage, was studied and implemented a distributed memory solution using MPI, where multiple processes will run to explore coarse-grained parallelism.
allprojects.roadmap:
This project was a deep dive into high-performance computing (HPC), focused on optimizing a particle simulation program. The goal was to significantly improve the code's performance by applying a range of advanced optimization techniques, moving from single-threaded efficiency to multi-threaded and finally to a distributed memory parallel solution. This was a comprehensive, three-phase effort to master code performance from the ground up.

The core technical challenge was a multi-faceted approach to performance optimization. In Phase 1, the focus was on sequential code improvements. I performed detailed profiling to identify bottlenecks and optimized the code's logic by simplifying formulas and reducing redundant calculations. The most significant challenge was optimizing for the memory hierarchy, where I used Loop Block Optimization to improve spatial locality and minimize cache misses. I also experimented with various compiler flags like -O2 and -O3 to find the optimal balance between performance and compiler-introduced overhead.

 In Phase 2, I moved to shared-memory parallelism using OpenMP. The main hurdle was identifying and protecting critical sections to prevent data races without introducing excessive synchronization overhead. I strategically used the reduction directive for variables, avoiding less efficient directives like atomic and critical. I studied the scalability of the solution, analyzing metrics like speedup and CPI (Cycles Per Instruction) to understand how performance was affected by the number of threads and potential issues like the Memory Wall and load imbalance. 

 In phase 3 was the most complex: migrating the solution to a distributed memory architecture using MPI (Message Passing Interface). This required rethinking the entire program flow to accommodate multiple processes running on different nodes. I implemented a data decomposition strategy, where each process was assigned a specific chunk of the particles to compute. The major challenge here was managing inter-process communication for data dependencies. I used MPI_Bcast to distribute initial data and MPI_Allreduce to aggregate the final Pot value and acceleration array from all processes, which was crucial for maintaining data consistency.

This project was an incredible learning experience in parallel and distributed computing. It provided hands-on expertise with OpenMP and MPI, teaching me how to analyze and solve real-world performance bottlenecks. I learned the critical difference between shared and distributed memory paradigms and the trade-offs of each. The project also solidified my skills in performance profiling and understanding hardware architecture, particularly the memory hierarchy. While the MPI-only implementation scaled better, the combined OpenMP + MPI solution achieved the best overall execution times, demonstrating the power of a hybrid approach. A key area for future improvement would be to explore more advanced MPI communication patterns and refine the load balancing to further minimize idle time and communication overhead, aiming for a more linear speedup with an increasing number of processes. Other option could be adapting the code for a  CUDA approach in order to execute  parallel tasks with substantial performance gains on GPU compatible workloads.

allprojects.name: Japanese Kanji : Flashcards

allprojects.roadmap:
I developed Kanji Flashcards, a mobile application designed to help users learn and master Japanese Kanji. My motivation was to create a simple yet effective tool that leveraged the proven method of active recall through digital flashcards. The app allows users to create their own custom flashcard decks, flip cards to reveal the answer, and manage their personal learning collection. This project was a practical exercise in building a focused, user-friendly mobile application from the ground up.

The primary challenge was designing an intuitive and efficient user experience for creating and managing content. While the core flipping mechanic was straightforward, the real complexity lay in building a robust system for user-generated content. I had to design a database to store each user's flashcards, ensuring that custom-made decks were easy to create, edit, and categorize. The user interface had to be clean and responsive, making it simple for learners to add new Kanji, associated readings, and meanings without a steep learning curve. This required meticulous attention to UI/UX design and data modeling to support the core functionality.

This project was a fantastic learning experience in mobile application development with Java. It taught me the importance of focusing on a single, core feature and perfecting it before adding more complexity. I gained practical experience in designing a database schema for user-specific data and building an interface for content management. If I were to improve this project, I would integrate it with a public Kanji API to auto-populate card data, reducing the manual effort for users. I would also add features like spaced repetition to optimize the learning process and a simple quiz mode to test a user's knowledge more formally.

allprojects.name: HP-SOUNDS

allprojects.roadmap:
I developed an immersive mobile application using Flutter that allows users to explore the magical world of Harry Potter. My goal was to create a digital sanctuary where fans could navigate iconic locations like Hogwarts and Diagon Alley while listening to ambient sounds tailored for studying, sleeping, or relaxation. This project was a fusion of user-centric design and mobile development, bringing the enchanting universe to life on a mobile device.

The primary technical challenge was creating a seamless, interactive experience. I used Flutter's rich animation and custom widget capabilities to build a dynamic UI that transitions smoothly between locations. The most complex feature was the interactive map. I had to design a system where a user could navigate from inside Hogwarts to Hogsmeade or other places like Grimmauld Place. This required careful management of screen states and location data. Another hurdle was implementing a reliable audio playback system for the background sounds, ensuring they played continuously and without interruption.

This project was a fantastic learning experience in mobile app development with Flutter. I gained expertise in state management, asynchronous programming for handling audio streams, and designing an intuitive user interface for a content-rich application. I also learned how to use third-party packages to extend Flutter's core functionality. If I were to improve this project, I would integrate more dynamic elements, such as weather effects that change with the user's location, and add a feature where users can customize their own soundscapes by combining different ambient tracks.

allprojects.name: CG2022-23
allprojects.description: Creation of a solar system with planet textures, rotation and translation movements of objects following catmull-curves.
allprojects.roadmap:
This project was a deep dive into the fundamentals of computer graphics using C++, C, and OpenGL. My goal was to build a dynamic and visually rich scene of a solar system, going beyond basic animation to implement advanced rendering techniques. This involved creating models with realistic textures, lighting, and complex motion paths, all rendered with modern OpenGL methods.

The main technical challenge was the implementation of a sophisticated rendering pipeline from scratch. A key part of this was Phase 4, where I had to programmatically generate texture coordinates and normals for each vertex of the 3D models. This was essential for applying textures correctly and allowing surfaces to react realistically to light. I also implemented different types of lighting—point, directional, and spot—reading their properties from XML files to make the scene configurable.

Beyond static rendering, I focused on advanced animation. I added new translation and rotation elements to the engine, using Catmull-Rom curves to define complex, smooth trajectories for objects. This allowed me to create a convincing animation of a comet traveling through the solar system. The comet itself was a significant challenge, as I had to construct its form using Bezier Patches, which required a deep understanding of parametric surfaces. A crucial optimization throughout this project was moving from the older immediate mode rendering to using Vertex Buffer Objects (VBOs), which significantly improved performance by offloading data to the GPU.

This project was a comprehensive learning experience in computer graphics programming. I gained expertise in 3D modeling fundamentals, advanced animation, and modern rendering techniques. I learned how to work with different lighting models, apply textures to complex geometries, and optimize performance using VBOs. This project solidified my understanding of how a rendering engine works at a low level. If I were to improve this project, I would explore implementing more advanced techniques like shadow mapping to create realistic shadows from the light sources and particle effects to give the comet a visible tail

allprojects.name: DNS-system
allprojects.description: A simulated DNS system on CORE network emulator.
allprojects.roadmap:
This project was a deep dive into building a robust, distributed network system for name resolution, much like a simplified DNS. The goal was to establish a resilient and fault-tolerant communication framework between multiple server and client components. The system was designed to handle client queries, inter-server communication, and dynamic data synchronization, all while addressing common network challenges like timeouts, data fragmentation, and concurrency.

The core technical challenge was orchestrating reliable communication across multiple layers and components. I implemented socket-based communication using both UDP (for client-to-primary-server queries) and TCP (for server-to-server data transfer). A key challenge was handling primary server inactivity. I implemented a 5-second timeout on the client-side, informing the user if a connection couldn't be established. On the server, I used multithreading to enable concurrent operations: one thread to handle client queries and another to listen for a secondary server to initiate a zone transfer.

The zone transfer itself presented a unique challenge: managing the process and gracefully handling timeouts. I created a dedicated thread on the primary server that listened for a 'FIN' message from the secondary server, which would be sent if the zone transfer timed out. This allowed the primary server to abort the transfer and initiate a new attempt. Another significant hurdle was handling large responses that exceeded the fixed 1KB DNS message size. I designed a fragmentation algorithm to split large responses into 432-byte packets, with the server informing the client of the total number of packets to expect. This ensured that the client could reconstruct the full, correct response.

In the second phase, I added a new layer to the system: a Stub Resolver (SR). This component was designed with a complex iterative communication loop that would dynamically choose the best server (primary, secondary, or stub) to resolve a query. The SR would try to connect to different servers, and if a connection failed, it would use a flag to track the failure and move on to the next server in a resilient, fall-back process.

This project was a comprehensive learning experience in network programming, concurrency, and fault-tolerant system design. It gave me a deep, practical understanding of how distributed systems operate at a low level, from raw socket communication to the intricacies of multithreading and data synchronization. I learned how to implement custom protocols to solve real-world problems like data fragmentation. The iterative communication logic in the SR was a key takeaway, teaching me how to build resilient software that can navigate network failures gracefully. If I were to improve this project, I would implement more sophisticated load balancing among the servers and add a more robust, persistent logging system to better track network events and performance.

allprojects.name: Famafeira
allprojects.description: A marketplace web app to handle fairs, stands and products. Famafeira is also a place to sell and buy products and services.
allprojects.roadmap:
I developed Famafeira, a marketplace web application designed to handle the unique dynamics of fairs, stands, and products. The goal was to create a comprehensive platform where vendors could manage their stands and products, and users could browse, buy, and sell. I chose to build this application using a Model-View-ViewModel (MVVM) architectural pattern with Razor Views, as it provided a clean separation of concerns and a structured approach to development. This was a personal project to master a robust and scalable web development framework.

The primary technical challenge was implementing the MVVM pattern within the .NET framework using Razor Views. Unlike a traditional MVC setup, Razor Views simplifies the structure by combining the view and controller logic into a single file, but it still requires a clear separation for testing and maintainability. I used C# for the backend logic, handling data models and business rules, and JavaScript for dynamic front-end interactions without full page reloads. Another significant hurdle was designing and interacting with the MySQL database to model the relationships between fairs, stands, and products. I had to ensure data integrity and create an efficient schema that could support various queries for searching, filtering, and displaying products.

This project was an excellent learning experience in full-stack web development, particularly in applying the MVVM pattern and working within the .NET ecosystem. It honed my skills in C# and JavaScript and gave me practical experience in database design with MySQL. I learned how to build a dynamic and responsive web application while adhering to a strict architectural pattern, which is crucial for building maintainable and scalable software. If I were to improve this project, I would implement a real-time chat feature for communication between buyers and sellers and explore integrating a payment gateway to handle transactions directly within the platform.

allprojects.name: Pack My Bag
allprojects.description: PackMyBag is a clothing rental service directly at the travel destination, eliminating the need to carry luggage. The solution promotes sustainability and convenience for travelers.
allprojects.roadmap:
PackMyBag is a full-stack web application for a clothing rental service, designed to promote sustainability and convenience for travelers. The objective was to build a highly scalable and resilient system using a modern microservices architecture, capable of handling everything from user authentication and product catalogs to orders and real-time notifications. This project was a comprehensive exercise in developing a complex, cloud-native application.

The core challenge was orchestrating the communication between numerous, independent services and deploying them in a dynamic cloud environment. The architecture of the application counts with 7 SpringBoot microservices for specific functions: notifications, users handling and authentication, stylist recommendations, catalog products, orders, user products favorites, and users carts. To manage communication, it was implemented an Express API Gateway  to redirect requests to thre correct microservice(s), and a middleware to handle JWT-based authentication for validation and protecting some routes.

A crucial aspect of the architecture was maintaining data consistency between microservices. It was used Kafka as a message broker for asynchronous communication, for example, to notify users about product availability changes or to alert them when an order status was updated.

A significant deployment challenge was dynamically configuring the frontend to communicate with the API Gateway's external IP, which could change in a cloud environment. I solved this using Ansible to automatically retrieve the API Gateway's IP and inject it into the frontend's configuration during the Docker build process. The entire system was deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), with Nginx acting as a web server to serve the Vue.js frontend and a PostgreSQL database on a dedicated pod with persistent storage.

This project was a good practical exercise in modern microservices architecture and cloud-native development. I gained invaluable hands-on experience with Docker, Kubernetes, and Ansible for automated, reproducible deployments. The project solidified my understanding of event-driven architectures using Kafka and the importance of a centralized API Gateway for managing a distributed system. I also honed my skills in backend development with Spring Boot and frontend with Vue.js and Vuex. A key area for improvement would be to implement a more robust monitoring and logging solution across all microservices to gain deeper insights into performance and potential bottlenecks in production.

allprojects.name: Vector Race
allprojects.description: Vector Race is a simulation project that visualizes different AI pathfinding algorithms competing in a race. The project uses multithreading to run each AI algorithm simultaneously, allowing for a real-time comparison of their efficiency and performance.
allprojects.roadmap:
Vector Race is a simulation project that visualizes different AI pathfinding algorithms competing to solve a maze. My goal was to create an interactive tool to demonstrate and compare the efficiency of popular search algorithms in real-time. The project is a fusion of AI concepts, concurrency, and dynamic visualization, all brought to life through a racing simulation.

The main technical challenge was creating a system where multiple, complex algorithms could run and be visualized simultaneously without interfering with each other. I used multithreading to run each AI algorithm (DFS, BFS, A*, Greedy Best-First Search) concurrently. This ensured a fair race and allowed for a true real-time comparison of their performance. The visualization layer, built with Pygame, was particularly challenging. I had to design it to dynamically display the progress of each 'car' and highlight the paths they calculated, all while updating a scoreboard with key metrics like path cost and search time. A unique aspect was the dynamic cost function, where collisions with obstacles incurred a penalty of 25, providing a more realistic and complex scenario for the algorithms to navigate.

This project was a comprehensive learning experience in multithreading, AI search algorithms, and game-like visualization. It provided a practical understanding of the trade-offs between different algorithms, such as A*'s heuristic-driven efficiency versus BFS's guarantee of finding the shortest path. I learned how to manage concurrent processes and handle real-time data updates in a graphical environment. If I were to improve this project, I would add more advanced algorithms like Dijkstra's or Bidirectional Search, and implement a feature for users to design their own custom mazes to see how the algorithms perform in different scenarios.
functionalities: Perform car races and check for AI pathfinding algorithm performances

allprojects.name: streaming-service-esr
allprojects.description: This repository contains a real-time Over-the-Top (OTT) media streaming service implemented on an application overlay network. The project aims to provide efficient multimedia content delivery by circumventing common network issues like congestion, resource limitations, bandwidth, and latency.
allprojects.roadmap:
This project presents the architectural and design strategies for a real-time media streaming service implemented on an application overlay network. My goal was to provide an efficient and resilient multimedia content delivery system by creating a custom network architecture that bypasses common issues like network congestion and latency. I prototyped the system using the CORE network emulator to simulate the physical network and deliver video to a set of clients, proving the concept in a controlled environment.

The core technical challenge was building a dynamic and intelligent overlay network. The service is built on a custom set of components: a Client for user interaction, a Server for content storage, a Rendezvous Point (RP) for managing the network topology and selecting optimal paths, and Intermediate Nodes for forwarding content. A key feature was the RP's role in running algorithms to find the best content distribution paths based on real-time metrics, such as the lowest travel time.

A significant implementation hurdle was the choice of transport protocol. While UDP was initially considered for its low latency, its unreliability led to significant packet loss, compromising the video stream. I switched to TCP, which, despite introducing higher latency, guaranteed packet delivery and order, ensuring a stable video feed. The system also used a custom protocol where servers would periodically send a unicast message to the RP to update their status and content list. For new clients, a request was flooded through the network to find an existing stream, and if none was found, the RP would initiate a new unicast stream.

This project provided a deep, practical understanding of network architecture, distributed systems, and content delivery networks (CDNs). It demonstrated my ability to design and implement a custom networking protocol and make critical architectural decisions based on real-world constraints. The use of a network emulator was crucial for testing and validating the system's behavior in various scenarios. While the TCP implementation stabilized the video, it introduced latency. If I were to improve this project, I would implement a multi-path routing algorithm to reroute packets if a node in the selected path fails, thereby improving the system's resilience and reducing the impact of single-point failures.

allprojects.name: System for managing the residential electrical network
allprojects.description: Developed a multi-agent system to manage energy distribution across a residential network using renewable sources. The system simulates coordination between agents—energy source, scheduler, distributor, and autonomous houses—to optimize energy usage, reduce variability from renewable production, and ensure fair load distribution.
allprojects.roadmap: The project was motivated by the desire to explore how a multi-agent system could intelligently manage energy distribution in a residential network relying on renewable sources, whose variability makes coordination difficult. By modeling each house, the energy source, the scheduler, and the distributor as autonomous agents, the goal was to simulate cooperation, optimize resource usage, and reduce the negative impact of inconsistent energy production. Throughout development, several challenges emerged, including designing a reliable asynchronous communication protocol between agents, implementing a synchronous scheduling phase within an otherwise asynchronous architecture, and ensuring correct coordination between agents with potentially conflicting objectives. Additional challenges involved simulating realistic energy production and consumption patterns, managing battery-charging logic, and prioritizing energy allocation under fluctuating supply. These obstacles led to significant learning, particularly in the design of distributed and hybrid agent architectures, the creation of structured message-passing protocols using JADE, and the implementation of cooperative behaviors in dynamic environments. The project strengthened understanding of resource scheduling, energy modeling, autonomy, and system scalability, while also reinforcing the importance of clear communication rules and robust coordination strategies in multi-agent systems.
